name: Concept true/false (or multiple-choice) with one-to-three-sentence justification
theory_paragraphs:
These questions sample the \term{vocabulary layer} of the whole course, so the theory to master is a set of crisp definitions. \term{CIA triad}: \term{confidentiality} = protection from unauthorized \emph{disclosure} (a read leak), \term{integrity} = protection from unauthorized \emph{modification} (output correct per specification), \term{availability} = protection from \emph{loss of use} (DoS attacks availability). \term{Privacy} is not a synonym of confidentiality: it concerns information \emph{about individuals} and includes control, context and metadata. The \term{Saltzer--Schroeder principles} are a favourite trap source and the list must be memorized \emph{exactly} --- there are eight:
\begin{tightitem}
\item \term{Least privilege}: every subject gets only the rights its task needs (fine-grained permissions).
\item \term{Fail-safe defaults}: default is deny; enumerate privileges (allowlists), not prohibitions.
\item \term{Economy of mechanism}: keep the security mechanism/TCB as \emph{simple and small} as necessary (KISS).
\item \term{Complete mediation}: the reference monitor checks every operation.
\item \term{Open design} (Kerckhoffs): the attacker knows the algorithms; only the key is secret --- \imp{no security through obscurity}.
\item \term{Separation of privilege}: require collusion of two parties for a sensitive action.
\item \term{Least common mechanism}: minimize mechanisms shared by (and coupling) different users, since shared mechanisms are potential information channels.
\item \term{Psychological acceptability}: unusable security gets bypassed.
\end{tightitem}
\term{Defense in depth} (overlapping, independent layers of mechanisms) is \imp{not one of the eight} --- it is a separate doctrine, and pairing it with the Saltzer--Schroeder list is exactly the wrong-principle trap this unit trains.

Authentication and access-control facts: the three \term{authentication factors} are something you \emph{are} (biometrics), \emph{know} (password, PIN), \emph{have} (token, card); two-factor means two \emph{independent categories} --- a password plus a PIN is still one factor. \term{Salts} are random, per-user and \imp{public, non-secret}; they defeat precomputation/rainbow tables and force per-user work ($O(M\cdot N)$ instead of $O(M+N)$ for $M$ candidates and $N$ users), they do not make weak passwords strong. \term{DAC}: owner sets permissions; \term{MAC}: central authority (e.g. Bell--LaPadula). \term{ACL} = matrix column per object (easy per-object review, simple revocation, vulnerable to \term{confused deputy}); \term{capability} = unforgeable name+privilege bundle per principal (no confused deputy, but review/delegation/revocation are hard).

Network-security definitions: a \term{packet-filtering firewall} drops whole packets based on \emph{header metadata only} (src/dest IP and port, protocol, interface) --- it \imp{cannot filter payload content}; content filtering needs an \term{application-level gateway}/proxy or deep packet inspection. A \term{stateful inspection firewall} additionally tracks the TCP connection table. IDS deployment: \term{NIDS} (on the network, cheap, transparent, but suffers inconsistent interpretation and cannot read TLS), \term{HIDS} (per host, sees what the host sees, handles encryption), log-based (cheap, no real-time). Detection styles: \term{signature-based} (blacklist of known attacks --- \imp{misses new attacks}), \term{specification-based} (whitelist of allowed behaviour), \term{anomaly-based} (learned model of normal --- high false positives), \term{behavioural} (flags effects of compromise). Every detector has \term{false positives} and \term{false negatives}; the \term{base-rate fallacy} means that with rare attacks even a small false-positive rate makes most alerts false alarms. DoS mechanics: \term{ICMP/UDP floods} exhaust \emph{bandwidth} (fixable only upstream --- victim-side dropping fails because \imp{the upstream link is already congested}); a \term{SYN flood} exhausts the server's \emph{pending-connection table} (state exhaustion), \imp{possible with less bandwidth than the victim}; defences are timeouts, per-IP limits and \term{SYN cookies}. \term{Reflection/amplification} abuses UDP spoofing (a 60-byte DNS query yields up to 4~KB response); \term{ingress filtering} (BCP~38) at the attacker's ISP blocks spoofed sources.

Systems and software facts: \term{stack canaries} place a random value between locals and the saved return address and \emph{detect} its change on return --- they miss overwrites that hijack before the return or leak the canary. \term{W $\oplus$ X / NX}: data pages non-executable, blocks injected shellcode but not ROP or data-only attacks. \term{ASLR} randomizes layout; it fails on pointer leaks, and stack-only ASLR preserves code addresses and relative offsets. \term{Guard pages} are MMU-illegal pages that abort on any access. \term{Side channels} are \emph{passive, non-invasive} observations of byproducts (time, cache, power); \term{fault injection} (e.g. Rowhammer) is \emph{active} and flips state. Malware taxonomy: a \term{virus} needs a host program and user action to spread, a \term{worm} self-propagates over the network, \term{polymorphic} malware rewrites itself to evade signatures. Web facts: the \term{SOP} isolates origins (scheme, domain, port); \term{HttpOnly} hides a cookie from JavaScript, \term{Secure} restricts it to HTTPS, \term{SameSite=Strict} sends it only same-site; parameterized queries are the correct SQLi defence.
theory_cheatsheet: CIA: read leak = confidentiality, modification = integrity, loss of use = availability. Privacy $>$ confidentiality (about individuals, control, metadata).

Principles (all eight): least privilege = minimum rights; fail-safe defaults = deny by default; economy of mechanism = small/simple TCB; complete mediation = check every operation; open design = attacker knows all but the key; separation of privilege = need two parties; least common mechanism = minimize shared mechanisms; psychological acceptability = usable or bypassed. Defense in depth is a separate doctrine, not on the list. Wrong-principle pairing is the classic trap.
Factors: are/know/have; 2FA = two different categories. Salt: public, per-user, defeats rainbow tables, not weak passwords.

Firewalls: packet filter = headers only, never payload; stateful = + connection table; content filtering = application proxy/DPI. SYN flood = state exhaustion (pending table, works with less bandwidth); ICMP/UDP flood = bandwidth (only upstream/ISP can fix; ingress filtering kills spoofing).
IDS: signature detects only known attacks; anomaly = learned normal, many false positives; every detector has FP and FN; base-rate fallacy: rare attacks $\Rightarrow$ most alerts false.
Defences' limits: canary detects return-address overwrite only; NX blocks injected code, not ROP; ASLR fails on leaks. Side channel = passive observation; fault injection = active.
identify_givens: A battery of short standalone statements (typically 5--6 for the E-level Part~1), each making one claim about a security concept, mechanism or attack --- e.g.\ equating two notions (``Privacy is a synonym for confidentiality''), attributing a mechanism (``A packet filtering firewall filters out specific content''), or naming a design principle (``\ldots goes against the principle of economy of mechanism''). Variant: multiple-choice options A--D marked with the club symbol where zero, one or several options may be true and ``None of these answers are correct'' is offered.
identify_target: For each statement, decide true/false (or mark all true options) and justify the verdict in one to three sentences by naming the correct property, definition or principle and giving the key distinction or counterexample. Grading typically awards the point if the reasoning makes at least one of the listed correct points.
identify_keywords: classify them as true or false and explain your reasoning
None of these answers are correct
strategy_name: Name the concept, then give the distinguishing counterexample

algorithm.detail: Write down (mentally) the precise course definition of that concept, e.g.\ packet-filtering firewall = drop whole packets based on header metadata only, never payload; economy of mechanism = the security mechanism should not be more complex than necessary; anomaly-based IDS = learned model of normal behaviour, hence high false positives; SYN flood = exhaustion of the pending-connection table.

Check the usual mismatch patterns:
\begin{tightitem}
\item absolute quantifiers (``only'', ``all'', ``never'', ``necessarily''),
\item claimed synonyms between notions of different scope (privacy vs.\ confidentiality),
\item swapped CIA properties (a read violation is confidentiality, not integrity),
\item a real bad practice paired with the \term{wrong named principle} (or a non-principle like defense in depth presented as one of the eight Saltzer--Schroeder principles),
\item a mechanism attributed to the wrong layer (content filtering needs DPI, not packet filtering) or wrong resource (SYN flood exhausts state, not bandwidth).
\end{tightitem}

Mark \emph{true} only if the statement is correct as written, including the named principle and quantifiers; a statement whose underlying observation is right but whose justification names the wrong principle is \emph{false}. For club-marked multiple choice, judge each option A--D \term{independently} --- several (or none) may be true, and never select ``None of these answers are correct'' together with another option.

In 1--3 sentences: state the verdict, give the correct definition, and name the distinguishing counterexample or correction, e.g.\ ``False: students only need read access to most pages, so this violates \term{least privilege}; economy of mechanism means the mechanism should not be more complex than necessary.'' \imp{Aim to hit at least one of the grading scheme's accepted points} --- give the sharpest distinction, not an essay.

variations.name: Single T/F battery with reasoning (2022 style)
variations.detail: Six independent statements, each classified and justified; grading accepts any one of several listed correct points. Trap: some statements are false because of the \term{mechanism or principle named}, not because the intuition is wrong --- so always check the justification clause, not just the headline claim.

variations.name: Multiple-true club format (dasak19 Part I)
variations.detail: Options A--D under a topic header (Concepts/CIA, Authentication, Cryptography, Memory safety, Malware, IDS/Firewalls) are graded \term{independently}; zero, one or several may be true. E.g.\ on IDS/firewalls all of these are true: signature IDS detects only known intrusions, firewalls do not stop internal threats, detection necessarily has false positives/negatives. ``None of these answers are correct'' exists to separate ``all false'' from ``unanswered''.

variations.name: Wrong-principle pairing trap
variations.detail: The statement describes a genuine security mistake but attributes it to the wrong Saltzer--Schroeder principle (economy of mechanism instead of least privilege, or vice versa) --- or invokes a principle that is not in the canonical eight at all. Adapt Step~3: verify the \term{named principle's definition} against the exact list, not just whether the practice is bad --- the verdict is False whenever the pairing is wrong.

variations.name: Synonym/quantifier trap
variations.detail: Words like ``synonym'', ``only'', ``necessarily'', ``never'' make a roughly-true statement false: privacy is broader than confidentiality; message authentication does \emph{not} require encrypting the content (only the digest is signed/MACed); a MAC gives integrity and \imp{no confidentiality}. Test the edge cases against the quantifier.

original_problem: Part 1, true/false with reasoning: ``A company replaces its signature-based IDS with an anomaly-based IDS and configures its new deep-packet-inspection firewall to read the content of TLS-encrypted web sessions, so that both previously unseen attacks can be detected with few false positives and malicious payloads inside encrypted traffic can be filtered at the perimeter.'' Classify the statement as true or false and explain your reasoning.

original_steps.work: The statement tests IDS detection styles and firewall capabilities; it makes two linked claims: (a) an anomaly-based IDS detects previously unseen attacks \emph{with few false positives}, and (b) a DPI firewall can read the \emph{content} of TLS-encrypted traffic.

Recall definitions: an \term{anomaly-based IDS} learns a model of normal behaviour and flags deviations --- it can indeed detect novel attacks, but at the price of \emph{many false positives}, since unusual-but-legitimate behaviour is flagged. \term{TLS} encrypts the payload end-to-end, so a middlebox sees only ciphertext and header metadata; \term{deep packet inspection} of the plaintext content is \imp{impossible without terminating TLS} (a man-in-the-middle proxy or endpoint visibility).

Traps found: (a) swaps the signature/anomaly trade-off --- novelty detection is bought \emph{at the cost of} false positives, so ``few false positives'' contradicts the definition; the \term{base-rate fallacy} makes it worse for rare attacks. (b) attributes plaintext visibility to a network middlebox on encrypted traffic --- reading TLS content would require breaking the encryption or acting as a trusted interception proxy, which a plain DPI firewall does not do; \term{HIDS} sees the plaintext because it sits at the endpoint.
Verdict: \textbf{False}. The stated detection benefit (few false positives) and the stated firewall capability (reading TLS content) are both wrong as written.

Justification to write: ``False. An \term{anomaly-based IDS} can detect previously unseen attacks, but its learned model of normality produces \emph{high} false-positive rates, and the base-rate fallacy amplifies this for rare attacks. A DPI firewall cannot read TLS content: the payload is end-to-end encrypted, so only ciphertext and header metadata are visible --- plaintext inspection requires terminating the TLS session (interception proxy) or endpoint visibility such as a \term{HIDS}.''
